    Chapter 5 · Databases

    Locking & Concurrency Control

    lockingpessimistic lockingoptimistic lockingSELECT FOR UPDATEFOR NO KEY UPDATEFOR SHARESKIP LOCKEDNOWAITlock_timeoutversion columncompare-and-swapatomic updateRETURNINGdeadlocklock orderingdeadlock_timeoutadvisory lockpg_advisory_xact_lockpg_try_advisory_lockjob queuedouble spendrace conditionwalletledgeridempotency key
    See also Transactions & Isolation Levels · Indexes · Celery with Redis as Broker · SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases · Django ORM in Depth · Transactions & Migrations
    On this page
    1. Pessimistic locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
    2. Optimistic locking: version column
    3. Atomic update: let the database do it
    4. Deadlocks and lock ordering
    5. Advisory locks
    6. Wallet withdrawal, three ways

    What: ways to stop concurrent transactions from breaking each other's data. Three families: pessimistic (lock first, then work), optimistic (work, then check nobody changed it), and atomic single statements (let the database do read+write in one step).

    ℹ Why it matters

    for a wallet or exchange, the classic question is "two withdrawal requests arrive at the same time, how do you prevent double spending?". Isolation levels alone (default Read Committed) do not solve it. See Transactions & Isolation.

    ↑ top

    Pessimistic locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

    Locks the selected rows until the txn ends. Other txns that try to UPDATE, DELETE or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the same rows wait. Plain SELECT is never blocked (MVCC).

    BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;   -- other writers wait here
-- app checks balance, computes...
UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;                                                 -- lock released
    Lock mode Use
    FOR UPDATE you will update/delete the row (strongest row lock)
    FOR NO KEY UPDATE you update non-key columns; does not block FK checks from child inserts (this is what a plain UPDATE takes)
    FOR SHARE read and make sure nobody changes it until commit; other FOR SHARE allowed

    Options for waiting:

    -- Fail immediately instead of waiting
SELECT * FROM wallets WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;    -- ERROR 55P03 if locked

-- Wait at most 2 seconds
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2s';

-- Skip rows that are locked: perfect for a job queue
BEGIN;
SELECT id, payload FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 10
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;          -- each worker gets different rows, no waiting
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running' WHERE id = ANY(:ids);
COMMIT;

    SKIP LOCKED gives a reliable job queue inside Postgres (no extra broker), as long as the volume is moderate. Pair it with a partial index ON jobs (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'.

    ↑ top

    Optimistic locking: version column

    No lock while the user/app thinks. At write time, update only if nobody changed the row since you read it.

    ALTER TABLE wallets ADD COLUMN version int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

SELECT balance, version FROM wallets WHERE id = 1;     -- 100, version 7

UPDATE wallets
SET balance = 70, version = version + 1
WHERE id = 1 AND version = 7;    -- 1 row → success; 0 rows → someone else won, retry
    • Always check the affected row count. 0 rows = conflict.
    • Good when conflicts are rare (editing a profile, admin forms, long "read → user edits → save" flows).
    • Bad when conflicts are frequent (hot wallet): many retries waste work.
    • Django: Wallet.objects.filter(id=1, version=7).update(balance=70, version=F("version") + 1) returns the row count.
    ↑ top

    Atomic update: let the database do it

    For counters and balances, the best answer is often one statement, no explicit lock, no retry:

    UPDATE wallets
SET balance = balance - 30
WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 30
RETURNING balance;      -- 0 rows → insufficient funds

    Why it's safe even in Read Committed: the UPDATE takes a row lock, and if another txn changed the row first, Postgres waits, then re-checks the WHERE on the newest version. So two concurrent withdrawals can never both pass balance >= 30 on stale data. Add CHECK (balance >= 0) as a final safety net.

    The trap is the read-modify-write in app code:

    w = Wallet.objects.get(id=1)        # ❌ lost update
w.balance -= 30
w.save()

Wallet.objects.filter(id=1, balance__gte=30).update(balance=F("balance") - 30)   # ✅ atomic
    ↑ top

    Deadlocks and lock ordering

    Two txns each hold a lock the other needs:

    A: UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;   -- locks 1
B: UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 2;   -- locks 2
A: UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2;   -- waits for B
B: UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 1;   -- waits for A → deadlock

    Postgres checks for deadlocks after deadlock_timeout (default 1s) and aborts one txn with SQLSTATE 40P01. The app should retry it.

    Prevent it:

    • Lock in a fixed order, e.g. by id: SELECT ... FROM wallets WHERE id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE; then do the updates.
    • Keep transactions short; no network calls while holding locks.
    • Use lock_timeout so a stuck txn fails fast instead of piling up waiters.
    ↑ top

    Advisory locks

    A lock on an app-chosen number, not on a row. Postgres doesn't know what it means; your code does.

    -- Transaction-level: released automatically at COMMIT/ROLLBACK (preferred)
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('payout:user:42'));

-- Try without waiting: returns true/false
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42);      -- session-level: you must pg_advisory_unlock(42)

    Use for: "only one cron instance runs this job", "only one payout process per user at a time", serializing work for a key that has no row yet. Caution: session-level advisory locks break with PgBouncer in transaction mode (the next txn may run on a different server connection); use the xact versions there.

    ↑ top

    Wallet withdrawal, three ways

    Requirement: withdraw 30 from wallet 1, never go below 0, and record it in a ledger.

    1. Atomic update (best default):

    BEGIN;
UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 30
WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 30
RETURNING balance;                 -- 0 rows → ROLLBACK, "insufficient funds"
INSERT INTO ledger (wallet_id, amount, kind) VALUES (1, -30, 'withdraw');
COMMIT;

    2. Pessimistic (when you need complex checks in app code, e.g. daily limit, KYC level):

    BEGIN;
SELECT balance, daily_withdrawn FROM wallets WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
-- app: check balance >= 30, check daily limit, fraud rules...
UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 30, daily_withdrawn = daily_withdrawn + 30 WHERE id = 1;
INSERT INTO ledger (wallet_id, amount, kind) VALUES (1, -30, 'withdraw');
COMMIT;

    3. Optimistic (low contention, or no long-held locks allowed):

    SELECT balance, version FROM wallets WHERE id = 1;     -- 100, v7
-- app: check 100 >= 30
BEGIN;
UPDATE wallets SET balance = 70, version = 8 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 7;
-- 0 rows → ROLLBACK and retry from the SELECT
INSERT INTO ledger (wallet_id, amount, kind) VALUES (1, -30, 'withdraw');
COMMIT;
    Atomic UPDATE Pessimistic FOR UPDATE Optimistic version
    Locks held very short whole txn very short
    Retries none none (but deadlock possible) yes, on conflict
    Complex app checks hard (only what fits in WHERE) easy easy
    Best for balances, counters, stock hot rows + complex rules rare conflicts, long user flows

    In all three, also use an idempotency key (unique constraint on request_id in the ledger) so a client retry does not withdraw twice.

    ✓ Key points
    • Read Committed + read-modify-write in the app = lost update. Use one of the three patterns.
    • FOR UPDATE blocks other writers on those rows, not plain readers.
    • SKIP LOCKED = job queue; NOWAIT / lock_timeout = fail fast.
    • Deadlocks: fixed lock order, short txns, retry on 40P01.
    • Advisory locks for app-level mutexes; prefer the xact version.
    ❝ Interview line

    "For a withdrawal I'd do a single conditional UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount RETURNING, so the check and the write are atomic, plus a unique idempotency key in the ledger. If the rules are too complex for a WHERE, I'd lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, and I'd always lock multiple rows in id order to avoid deadlocks."

    ⚠ Common trap

    thinking "it's inside a transaction, so it's safe". A transaction at Read Committed does not stop two requests from both reading balance 100 and both withdrawing. You need a lock, an atomic update, or a version check.

    Chapter 5 · Databases

    SQL vs NoSQL & Scaling Databases

    SQLNoSQLrelationaldocument storeMongoDBkey-valueRediswide-columnCassandraScyllaDBgraph databaseNeo4jnormalizationdenormalizationreplicationprimaryreplicaread replicasynchronous replicationasynchronous replicationreplication lagread-your-writesfailoverpartitioningshardingshard keyhot partitionreshardingconsistent hashingCitusconnection poolingPgBouncerN+1 queryselect_relatedprefetch_relatedjoinedloadselectinloadORM
    See also Indexes · Transactions & Isolation Levels · Locking & Concurrency Control · How to Run a System Design Interview · Kafka vs RabbitMQ
    On this page
    1. SQL vs NoSQL
    2. Normalization vs denormalization
    3. Replication
    4. Partitioning vs sharding
    5. Connection pooling (PgBouncer)
    6. The N+1 query problem

    What: how to choose a database type, and how to scale one when a single server is not enough: replication for reads, partitioning/sharding for size and writes, pooling for connections, and fixing ORM query patterns.

    ℹ Why it matters

    every system design round has a "data layer" part. A good answer starts with one Postgres, explains the bottleneck, and adds the smallest step that fixes it. See the SD framework.

    ↑ top

    SQL vs NoSQL

    Type Examples Data model Good for Weak at
    Relational (SQL) Postgres, MySQL tables, joins, schema money, orders, users: anything needing transactions and constraints horizontal write scaling (needs work)
    Document MongoDB JSON documents flexible / nested data read as one unit (product catalog, CMS) joins, multi-document transactions (possible but costly)
    Key-value Redis, DynamoDB key → value cache, sessions, rate limits, very fast lookups by key queries by anything other than the key
    Wide-column Cassandra, ScyllaDB partition key → sorted rows huge write volume, time series, messages, logs ad-hoc queries, joins, strong consistency (tunable)
    Graph Neo4j nodes + edges relationships many hops deep (fraud rings, recommendations) bulk aggregations

    Rule of thumb: Postgres by default (it also has jsonb, full-text search, partitioning). Add a specialized store when a clear requirement asks for it, often next to Postgres (Redis cache, Elasticsearch search, ClickHouse analytics).

    For a crypto exchange: balances, orders, ledger → Postgres (ACID). Order book in memory / Redis. Trade history and market data at high volume → time-series or columnar store.

    ↑ top

    Normalization vs denormalization

    • Normalization: each fact stored once (3NF). orders.user_id points to users; the user's name lives only in users. No update anomalies, smaller writes, but reads need joins.
    • Denormalization: copy data to avoid joins or recomputation. Faster reads, but you must keep copies in sync.
    -- Normalized: compute on read
SELECT u.id, count(o.id) FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id GROUP BY u.id;

-- Denormalized: keep a counter, update it in the same txn as the insert
UPDATE users SET orders_count = orders_count + 1 WHERE id = 7;

    Start normalized. Denormalize specific hot read paths (counters, cached totals, materialized views, read models built from events), and know who updates the copy.

    ↑ top

    Replication

    The primary takes all writes; replicas receive the changes (Postgres streams the WAL) and serve reads.

    writes ─► Primary ──WAL stream──► Replica 1 ◄─ reads
                   └────────────► Replica 2 ◄─ reads
    Async (default) Sync
    Commit returns when primary has written WAL locally at least one replica has also confirmed
    Write latency low higher (network round trip)
    Data loss on primary crash last few commits may be lost none (for confirmed standbys)
    Postgres setting default synchronous_standby_names + synchronous_commit = on (or remote_apply to make the change visible on the replica too)

    Replication lag: an async replica can be milliseconds to seconds behind. Problem: user updates their profile, the next page reads from a replica, and shows the old data.

    Fixes for read-your-writes:

    • Read from the primary for that user for a few seconds after they write (sticky flag in session/cookie).
    • Always read critical data (balances, order status) from the primary.
    • Track the WAL position: after a write, remember pg_current_wal_lsn(); only use a replica whose pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() has passed it.

    Also: replicas scale reads only; writes still hit one primary. Failover (Patroni, cloud managed) promotes a replica when the primary dies.

    Logical replication (row changes per table) is a different tool, used for migrations, partial copies and CDC (e.g. Debezium → Kafka).

    ↑ top

    Partitioning vs sharding

    Partitioning Sharding
    Where one Postgres server, one table split into child tables data split across many servers
    Goal manage huge tables: faster pruning, cheap deletes of old data scale writes and storage beyond one machine
    Transparent to app yes no (or via Citus / a proxy)
    Cross-part queries / txns normal SQL expensive or not supported 
    CREATE TABLE trades (
    id bigint, symbol text, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL, ...
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE trades_2026_10 PARTITION OF trades
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-01') TO ('2026-11-01');

-- WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-05' scans only trades_2026_10 (partition pruning)
-- Retention: DROP TABLE trades_2025_01;   instant, no huge DELETE

    Postgres supports RANGE, LIST and HASH partitioning. Note: a unique key or primary key must include the partition key.

    Choosing a shard key:

    • High cardinality and even distribution: user_id, account_id.
    • Matches the main queries: most queries should hit one shard (WHERE user_id = ?).
    • Avoid hot keys: created_at sends all new writes to the last shard; one huge market maker on account_id may need special handling.
    • Related data lives together: shard orders, wallets, ledger all by user_id so a user's txn stays on one shard.

    Resharding: with shard = hash(key) % N, changing N moves almost every key. Common fixes:

    • Create many logical shards (e.g. 1024) up front and map them to a few physical servers; to grow, move whole logical shards.
    • Consistent hashing: keys and nodes on a ring; adding a node moves only about 1/N of the keys (used by Cassandra, DynamoDB, cache clusters).

    Before sharding, try: indexes, query fixes, caching, read replicas, partitioning, a bigger machine. Sharding adds lasting complexity (cross-shard joins, distributed transactions, rebalancing).

    ↑ top

    Connection pooling (PgBouncer)

    Postgres starts one OS process per connection (several MB each). 50 app pods × 20 connections = 1000 connections, which hurts Postgres badly. A pooler keeps a small number of real server connections and shares them.

    PgBouncer mode A server connection is given to a client for Notes
    session the whole client session safe, but little sharing
    transaction one transaction most common; breaks session state: SET (use SET LOCAL), session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables; prepared statements need PgBouncer 1.21+ with max_prepared_statements
    statement one statement no multi-statement txns; rare

    Also keep app-side pools small (SQLAlchemy pool_size, Django CONN_MAX_AGE, Go db.SetMaxOpenConns). More connections than CPU cores rarely makes Postgres faster.

    ↑ top

    The N+1 query problem

    The ORM loads a list with 1 query, then runs 1 more query per row when you touch a relation. 100 orders → 101 queries.

    # Django: N+1
for order in Order.objects.all()[:100]:
    print(order.user.email)            # 1 query per order

# Fix: FK / one-to-one → JOIN in the same query
for order in Order.objects.select_related("user")[:100]:
    print(order.user.email)            # 1 query total

# Reverse FK / many-to-many → 2 queries: orders, then items WHERE order_id IN (...)
Order.objects.prefetch_related("items")

    # SQLAlchemy 2.0
from sqlalchemy.orm import joinedload, selectinload

stmt = select(Order).options(joinedload(Order.user))      # many-to-one: JOIN
stmt = select(Order).options(selectinload(Order.items))   # one-to-many: second query with IN (...)
orders = session.scalars(stmt).unique().all()

    Detect it: Django Debug Toolbar / nplusone, SQLAlchemy echo=True, or the same query repeated many times in pg_stat_statements. In Go (no ORM magic) the same bug is a query inside a loop; fix with one WHERE id = ANY($1) query and a map.

    ✓ Key points
    • Start with one Postgres; add replicas, partitioning, caches, then sharding, only when a bottleneck shows.
    • Async replicas lag: critical reads and read-your-writes go to the primary.
    • Partitioning is inside one server; sharding is across servers and changes your app.
    • Shard key = even, high cardinality, in most queries; plan for resharding (logical shards / consistent hashing).
    • PgBouncer in transaction mode; avoid session-level features.
    • N+1: select_related/joinedload for to-one, prefetch_related/selectinload for to-many.
    ❝ Interview line

    "I'd keep money data in Postgres for ACID. To scale reads I'd add async replicas but send read-your-writes and balance reads to the primary, put PgBouncer in front, partition big time-based tables, and shard by user_id only when one primary can't handle the writes."

    ⚠ Common trap

    "NoSQL scales, SQL doesn't." Postgres handles a lot on one machine with good indexes, replicas and partitioning, and NoSQL doesn't remove the need to pick a good partition key. Second trap: adding read replicas and forgetting replication lag.

    Chapter 6 · Networking

    Networking Overview

    2 pages. Each card says what the page covers and its key lines; open the page for the full depth.

    HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3

    three versions of the same protocol. The semantics are identical (GET/POST, status codes, headers). What changes is how bytes travel: text vs binary, how many requests share a connection, and TCP vs UDP.

    • HTTP/1.1: keep-alive, but one request at a time per connection → browsers open ~6 connections per host.
    • HTTP/2: binary frames, many streams on one TCP connection, HPACK headers. Still TCP head-of-line blocking on packet loss.
    • HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC (UDP): per-stream loss recovery, TLS 1.3 built in (1-RTT, 0-RTT resume), connection migration.
    • Same semantics (methods, status codes, headers) in all versions; only the transport/wire format changes.
    • gRPC needs HTTP/2 (streams + trailers) end to end → the load balancer must speak HTTP/2 to backends.
    Read the full page →

    Web & Networking Fundamentals

    the basic building blocks under every web backend: transport (TCP/UDP), security (TLS), naming (DNS), and the HTTP layer (methods, status codes, API styles, auth, CORS).

    • TCP = reliable, ordered, connection (3-way handshake). UDP = no handshake, no order, no retransmit (DNS, video, QUIC).
    • URL → DNS → TCP handshake → TLS → HTTP request → server/app/DB → response → render.
    • Safe = no side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). Idempotent = same result if repeated (safe + PUT, DELETE). POST and PATCH are not.
    • 401 = not authenticated, 403 = authenticated but not allowed. 502 = bad upstream answer, 504 = upstream timeout.
    • Server → client push: SSE (one-way, simple), WebSocket (two-way), long polling (fallback).
    • CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server; it doesn't protect your API from curl.
    Read the full page →

    Chapter 6 · Networking

    HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3

    HTTP/1.0HTTP/1.1HTTP/2HTTP/3QUICkeep-alivepersistent connectionpipelininghead-of-line blockingHOL blockingmultiplexingstreambinary framingHPACKQPACKserver push103 Early HintsALPNAlt-Svc0-RTT1-RTTTLS 1.3connection migrationconnection IDUDPgRPCTLS terminationload balancerh2c
    See also Web & Networking Fundamentals · Go Essentials & Gotchas · Django REST Framework
    On this page
    1. HTTP/1.0 → HTTP/1.1
    2. HTTP/2 (2015)
    3. HTTP/3 (2022, RFC 9114)
    4. Comparison
    5. What this means for a backend engineer

    What: three versions of the same protocol. The semantics are identical (GET/POST, status codes, headers). What changes is how bytes travel: text vs binary, how many requests share a connection, and TCP vs UDP.

    ℹ Why it matters

    it explains real performance questions ("why is my page slow on mobile?", "why does gRPC break behind this proxy?") and is a common "what's the difference" interview question.

    ↑ top

    HTTP/1.0 → HTTP/1.1

    • HTTP/1.0: a new TCP connection for every request. Each one pays the TCP (and TLS) handshake.
    • HTTP/1.1 (1997):
      • Keep-alive (persistent connections) by default: reuse one TCP connection for many requests.
      • Host header required → many sites on one IP (virtual hosting).
      • Chunked transfer encoding: stream a body without knowing its length.
      • Pipelining: send several requests without waiting, but responses must come back in order. One slow response blocks all others behind it (head-of-line blocking). Buggy proxies → browsers never enabled it.
    • Result: per connection, effectively one request in flight at a time. Browsers work around it by opening ~6 parallel connections per host. Old hacks: domain sharding, sprites, bundling files.
    HTTP/1.1, one connection:
  req A ──► ... resp A ◄──  req B ──► ... resp B ◄──     (serial)
HTTP/1.1, pipelining:
  req A, req B ──►   resp A (slow) ... resp B waits behind A   (HOL blocking)
    ↑ top

    HTTP/2 (2015)

    • Binary framing: messages are split into frames (HEADERS, DATA, ...), each tagged with a stream ID.
    • Multiplexing: many streams (request/response pairs) are interleaved on one TCP connection. A slow response no longer blocks others at the HTTP level.
    • HPACK header compression: static + dynamic tables, so repeated headers (cookies, user-agent) cost a few bytes.
    • Stream priority and flow control per stream and per connection.
    • Server push: server sends resources before they are asked for. Deprecated in practice (Chrome removed it in 2022); use 103 Early Hints / <link rel=preload> instead.
    • Negotiated via ALPN during the TLS handshake (h2). Browsers only use HTTP/2 over TLS; cleartext h2c exists for internal traffic.
    One TCP connection:
  [S1 HEADERS][S3 HEADERS][S1 DATA][S3 DATA][S5 HEADERS][S1 DATA] ...
   stream 1, 3, 5 interleaved → no HTTP-level HOL blocking

    The remaining problem: TCP head-of-line blocking. TCP delivers one ordered byte stream. If one packet is lost, TCP holds all later bytes until the retransmit arrives, even bytes belonging to other streams. On a lossy network, HTTP/2 with one connection can be worse than HTTP/1.1 with 6.

    packet loss on stream 1:
  TCP:  [S1 ✗][S3 ✓][S5 ✓]  → S3 and S5 wait for S1's retransmit (kernel buffers them)
    ↑ top

    HTTP/3 (2022, RFC 9114)

    HTTP/3 = HTTP semantics on QUIC, a transport built on UDP (QUIC runs in user space, not in the kernel).

    • Independent streams in the transport: a lost packet only blocks its own stream. No TCP HOL blocking.
    • TLS 1.3 is built into QUIC: transport + crypto handshake together → 1-RTT for a new connection (TCP + TLS 1.3 needs 2 RTT). 0-RTT on resumption (send data in the first packet; replayable, so only safe for idempotent requests).
    • Connection migration: connections are identified by a connection ID, not the IP/port 4-tuple. Phone moves Wi-Fi → 4G and the connection survives.
    • QPACK header compression (HPACK adapted for out-of-order streams).
    • Almost everything is encrypted, even transport headers → middleboxes can't mess with it.
    • Discovery: server advertises Alt-Svc: h3=":443" (or an HTTPS DNS record); the client tries QUIC and falls back to TCP if UDP is blocked.
    Handshake round trips before the first request:
  HTTP/1.1 or 2 + TLS 1.3:  TCP SYN/ACK (1 RTT) + TLS (1 RTT) = 2 RTT
  HTTP/3 (QUIC):            QUIC+TLS together              = 1 RTT   (0 RTT on resume)
    ↑ top

    Comparison

    HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3
    Transport TCP TCP QUIC over UDP
    Format text binary frames binary frames (QUIC streams)
    Requests per connection one at a time (pipelining unused) many multiplexed streams many multiplexed streams
    Connections per host (browser) ~6 1 1
    HOL blocking HTTP level + TCP level TCP level only none across streams
    Header compression none HPACK QPACK
    TLS optional (separate) in practice required (browsers) always, TLS 1.3 built in
    New-connection setup (with TLS 1.3) 2 RTT 2 RTT 1 RTT (0-RTT resume)
    Network change (Wi-Fi → 4G) reconnect reconnect connection migrates
    Server push no yes, deprecated in spec, rarely used
    ↑ top

    What this means for a backend engineer

    • gRPC needs HTTP/2 end to end: it uses streams for streaming RPCs and trailers for grpc-status. A proxy/load balancer that downgrades to HTTP/1.1 breaks it. Configure the LB for HTTP/2 to backends (e.g. Nginx grpc_pass, Envoy, AWS ALB with gRPC target group).
    • Load balancing gRPC/HTTP/2: one long-lived connection carries all requests, so an L4 (TCP) load balancer pins one client to one backend. Use an L7 LB (balances per request/stream) or client-side balancing.
    • TLS termination: usually at the edge (CDN, LB, Nginx). The edge can speak HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to clients and plain HTTP/1.1 to the app. Your Python/Go app often never sees HTTP/3.
    • When HTTP/3 helps: mobile and lossy/high-latency networks, users switching networks, many small parallel requests. Inside a data center (low loss, low RTT) the gain is small.
    • HTTP/3 costs: UDP may be blocked or rate-limited by firewalls, QUIC uses more CPU (user space, encrypted headers), and tooling/debugging is less mature.
    • Old HTTP/1.1 hacks (domain sharding, bundling everything) hurt with HTTP/2 because they defeat the single multiplexed connection.
    ✓ Key points
    • All versions keep the same methods, status codes and headers. Code at the handler level doesn't change.
    • HTTP/2 fixed HOL blocking at the HTTP layer; HTTP/3 fixed it at the transport layer.
    • QUIC's handshake merges transport + TLS → faster setup; 0-RTT data can be replayed, so only use it for idempotent requests.
    • Version is chosen with ALPN (h2) and Alt-Svc / DNS HTTPS records (h3), with fallback.
    ❝ Interview line

    "HTTP/1.1 handles one request at a time per connection, so browsers open several connections. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection with binary frames and header compression, but a lost TCP packet still blocks all streams. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC over UDP, so loss only affects one stream, the TLS 1.3 handshake is built in, and connections survive network changes, which helps most on mobile."

    ⚠ Common trap

    saying "HTTP/2 removed head-of-line blocking". It removed it at the HTTP level only. TCP still delivers bytes in order, so one lost packet stalls every stream on the connection; that is exactly what HTTP/3/QUIC fixes.

    Chapter 6 · Networking

    Web & Networking Fundamentals

    TCPUDPthree-way handshakeSYNACKFINTIME_WAITTLS 1.3TLS handshakecertificateSNIDNSrecursive resolverroot serverTLDauthoritative name serverTTLA recordCNAMEwhat happens when you type a URLRESTgRPCProtobufWebSocketSSEServer-Sent Eventslong pollingHTTP status codesidempotentsafe methodsPUT vs PATCHcookiesJWTsessionCORSpreflightOPTIONSsame-origin policy
    See also HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 · Redis Pub/Sub vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka · Request Lifecycle, Middleware & Signals · Django REST Framework
    On this page
    1. TCP vs UDP
    2. DNS resolution
    3. What happens when you type a URL
    4. API styles
    5. HTTP methods
    6. Status codes to know
    7. Cookies vs tokens (JWT)
    8. CORS

    What: the basic building blocks under every web backend: transport (TCP/UDP), security (TLS), naming (DNS), and the HTTP layer (methods, status codes, API styles, auth, CORS).

    ℹ Why it matters

    "what happens when you type a URL?" and "REST vs gRPC vs WebSocket?" are classic warm-up questions. Wrong status codes or non-idempotent retries are common real bugs.

    ↑ top

    TCP vs UDP

    TCP UDP
    Connection yes (handshake) no
    Reliability retransmits lost packets none (app handles it)
    Ordering ordered byte stream datagrams, any order
    Flow/congestion control yes no (app may add it)
    Header 20+ bytes 8 bytes
    Used by HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, DB connections, SSH DNS, video/voice, games, QUIC (HTTP/3)

    TCP 3-way handshake (1 RTT before data):

    client                     server
  │ ── SYN (seq=x) ──────────► │
  │ ◄── SYN-ACK (seq=y,ack=x+1)│
  │ ── ACK (ack=y+1) ────────► │   connection open; data can go with this ACK

    Close: FIN/ACK in each direction (4 steps). The side that closes first waits in TIME_WAIT (many short connections → port exhaustion; use keep-alive / connection pools).

    TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT, on top of TCP):

    ClientHello (ciphers, key share, SNI) ──►
◄── ServerHello (key share) + {certificate, signature, Finished}   (already encrypted)
Finished + first HTTP request ──►
    • Both sides compute the shared key from the key shares (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman → forward secrecy).
    • Client checks the certificate chain against trusted CAs and the hostname.
    • SNI tells the server which hostname you want (one IP, many certificates).
    • Resumption can use 0-RTT (replayable → only for idempotent requests). TLS 1.2 needed 2 RTT.
    ↑ top

    DNS resolution

    1. Browser cache → OS cache (/etc/hosts, stub resolver).
    2. Ask the recursive resolver (ISP, 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1). If cached, done.
    3. Resolver asks a root server → "ask the .com TLD servers".
    4. Asks the TLD server → "ask example.com's authoritative servers".
    5. Asks the authoritative server → A 93.184.216.34 (or CNAME → repeat for the target).
    6. Result is cached at every level for its TTL.

    Records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT, NS. Mostly UDP port 53 (TCP for large answers). Low TTL = faster failover, more queries.

    ↑ top

    What happens when you type a URL

    1. Parse the URL (scheme, host, port, path). Check HSTS → force HTTPS.
    2. DNS lookup → IP (steps above).
    3. TCP handshake to IP:443 (or QUIC for HTTP/3).
    4. TLS handshake: certificate check, keys, ALPN picks h2/http/1.1.
    5. HTTP request: GET /path with headers (Host, cookies, Accept, ...).
    6. Server side: CDN/load balancer → reverse proxy (Nginx) → app server (Gunicorn/uvicorn, Go net/http) → cache/DB → build response.
    7. Response: status, headers (Cache-Control, Set-Cookie), body.
    8. Browser renders: parse HTML → fetch CSS/JS/images (more requests, reuse the connection) → build DOM/CSSOM → layout → paint. JS runs.
    ↑ top

    API styles

    REST gRPC WebSocket SSE Long polling
    Direction request/response request/response + streaming (client, server, bidi) full duplex server → client only server → client (emulated)
    Transport HTTP/1.1 or 2 HTTP/2 HTTP/1.1 Upgrade, then raw frames over TCP plain HTTP, kept open repeated HTTP requests
    Format JSON (usually) Protobuf (binary, typed, generated code) any (text/binary) text data: events JSON
    Browser support native needs gRPC-Web proxy native native (EventSource, auto-reconnect) native
    Best for public/CRUD APIs, caching internal service-to-service, low latency, strict contracts chat, games, collaborative editing notifications, live feeds, LLM token streaming fallback when nothing else works
    Cost simple, cacheable tooling, harder to debug stateful connections, harder to scale (sticky/pub-sub fan-out) one-way only high overhead, latency

    Scaling note: WebSocket/SSE connections are long-lived and stateful. With many servers, use a pub/sub layer (e.g. Redis Pub/Sub) so any server can push to any user.

    ↑ top

    HTTP methods

    Method Safe Idempotent Note
    GET yes yes read; cacheable
    HEAD yes yes headers only
    OPTIONS yes yes CORS preflight
    PUT no yes replace the whole resource
    DELETE no yes second call may return 404, but the state is the same
    POST no no create / action; use an Idempotency-Key header for safe retries
    PATCH no no (not guaranteed) partial update ({"op": "increment"} isn't idempotent)

    Safe = doesn't change server state. Idempotent = doing it N times has the same effect as once. Retries (clients, proxies, queues) are only automatic-safe for idempotent methods.

    ↑ top

    Status codes to know

    Code Meaning
    200 OK / 201 Created / 204 No Content success (201 + Location header for new resources)
    301 / 308 permanent redirect (308 keeps the method)
    302 / 307 temporary redirect (307 keeps the method)
    304 Not Modified cache still valid (ETag / If-None-Match)
    400 Bad Request malformed input
    401 Unauthorized not authenticated (no/invalid credentials)
    403 Forbidden authenticated, but no permission
    404 Not Found no such resource
    409 Conflict state conflict (duplicate, version mismatch)
    422 Unprocessable Content valid syntax, failed validation (FastAPI uses it)
    429 Too Many Requests rate limited (Retry-After)
    500 Internal Server Error bug in your server
    502 Bad Gateway proxy got an invalid response from upstream (app crashed/closed)
    503 Service Unavailable overloaded / maintenance
    504 Gateway Timeout proxy got no response in time from upstream
    ↑ top

    Cookies vs tokens (JWT)

    • Session cookie: server stores the session (DB/Redis), the browser sends an opaque session ID cookie automatically. Easy to revoke. Set HttpOnly (no JS access → XSS-safe), Secure, SameSite (CSRF protection).
    • JWT: a signed token header.payload.signature with claims (sub, exp). The server verifies the signature, no DB lookup → stateless, good for microservices. Downsides: hard to revoke before exp (use short-lived access tokens + refresh tokens, or a denylist); the payload is only base64, not encrypted.
    • They're not opposites: a JWT can be stored in a cookie. Cookie = transport, JWT = token format.
    ↑ top

    CORS

    Browsers apply the same-origin policy: JS on app.com can't read responses from api.com (different scheme, host or port). CORS lets the server opt in with headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.com. For "non-simple" requests (e.g. PUT, JSON content type, custom headers like Authorization), the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request and checks the Access-Control-Allow-* headers. With credentials (cookies) you can't use * as the origin. CORS is only enforced by browsers; it isn't server-side security.

    ✓ Key points
    • TCP handshake costs 1 RTT, TLS 1.3 another 1 RTT → reuse connections (keep-alive, pools).
    • DNS is cached at every level by TTL; it's also a cheap way to do failover/geo-routing.
    • Choose the API style by direction and client: REST for public, gRPC internal, SSE for server push, WebSocket for two-way.
    • Make retried operations idempotent (PUT, or POST + Idempotency-Key).
    ❝ Interview line

    "When I type a URL, the browser resolves the name through DNS, opens a TCP connection, does a TLS handshake, sends the HTTP request, and the request passes through a load balancer and reverse proxy to the app, which may hit a cache or database before the response comes back and the browser renders it."

    ⚠ Common trap

    mixing up 401 and 403, or thinking CORS protects the API. 401 means "who are you?", 403 means "I know you, but no". CORS only stops a browser page from reading the response; any non-browser client ignores it, so you still need real auth.

    Chapter 7 · Go

    Go Overview

    1 pages. Each card says what the page covers and its key lines; open the page for the full depth.

    Go Essentials & Gotchas

    the Go concurrency toolkit (goroutines, channels, select, sync, context) plus the classic "predict the output" gotchas.

    • Goroutine = ~2 KB growable stack, scheduled by Go (GMP: many G on few OS threads M via P = GOMAXPROCS).
    • Unbuffered send blocks until a receiver is ready; receive from a closed chan → zero value, ok=false; nil chan blocks forever.
    • Only the sender closes a channel. Send on closed chan → panic.
    • append may share the backing array → two slices from one base can overwrite each other.
    • An interface holding a typed nil pointer is not == nil. Return a literal nil error.
    • Concurrent map writes → fatal error (not recoverable). Use sync.Mutex or sync.Map; run tests with -race.
    Read the full page →
    ↑ Back to top⌂ Home
    ← PreviousWeb & Networking FundamentalsNext →Go Essentials & Gotchas
    ← → to turn pages · / to search
    Chapter 7 · Go

    Go Essentials & Gotchas

    GogoroutineGMP schedulerchannelbuffered channelunbuffered channelclosenil channelselecttime.Aftercontextcontext.WithTimeoutcontext.WithCancelsync.WaitGroupsync.Mutexsync.RWMutexsync.Onceerrgroupslice appendbacking arrayloop variable captureGo 1.22nil interfacetyped nildeferconcurrent map writessync.Mapmap iteration ordergoroutine leakrace detector
    See also Async / Await · HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
    On this page
    1. Goroutines vs threads
    2. Channels
    3. select, timeouts, context
    4. sync package and errgroup
    5. Gotchas: predict the output

    What: the Go concurrency toolkit (goroutines, channels, select, sync, context) plus the classic "predict the output" gotchas.

    ℹ Why it matters

    Go interviews almost always include one concurrency question and one gotcha snippet. Compare with Python's model in Async / Await.

    ↑ top

    Goroutines vs threads

    Goroutine OS thread
    Start cost ~2 KB stack, grows as needed ~1–8 MB fixed stack
    Scheduled by Go runtime (user space) OS kernel
    Switch cost cheap expensive (kernel)
    How many 100k+ is fine thousands

    GMP scheduler: G = goroutine, M = OS thread, P = logical processor with a run queue (GOMAXPROCS, default = CPU cores). An M needs a P to run Gs; idle Ps steal work from others. A G blocked in a syscall releases its P so another M keeps running Gs. Unlike Python asyncio, goroutines run in parallel on multiple cores and are preempted (no await needed).

    ↑ top

    Channels

    ch := make(chan int, 3) // buffered: send blocks only when full
ch <- 1
ch <- 2
close(ch)            // only the sender closes
for v := range ch {  // range stops after close + drain
    fmt.Print(v, " ")
}
v, ok := <-ch
fmt.Println(v, ok)   // 1 2 0 false
    Operation nil channel open channel closed channel
    send blocks forever blocks until receiver (unbuffered) / buffer space panic
    receive blocks forever blocks until value zero value, ok=false
    close panic ok panic
    • Unbuffered = synchronization point (sender and receiver meet). Buffered = queue of size N.
    • Nil channel blocking is useful: set a channel var to nil in a select to disable that case.
    ↑ top

    select, timeouts, context

    select {
case r := <-res:
    fmt.Println(r)
case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
    fmt.Println("timeout")
}

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 50*time.Millisecond)
defer cancel() // always call cancel, or the timer leaks until it fires
select {
case <-time.After(time.Second):
    fmt.Println("finished")
case <-ctx.Done():
    fmt.Println(ctx.Err()) // context deadline exceeded
}
    • select picks a random ready case; default makes it non-blocking.
    • context: pass ctx as the first argument down the call chain; long work checks ctx.Done(). Cancelling a parent cancels all children. Used for request deadlines in HTTP handlers and DB calls.

    Worker that stops on close or cancel:

    func worker(ctx context.Context, jobs <-chan int, results chan<- int) {
    for {
        select {
        case j, ok := <-jobs:
            if !ok {
                return // jobs closed
            }
            results <- j * 2
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return
        }
    }
}
    ↑ top

    sync package and errgroup

    Tool Use
    sync.WaitGroup wait for N goroutines: Add(1) before go, defer Done(), Wait()
    sync.Mutex exclusive lock around shared state
    sync.RWMutex many readers or one writer (read-heavy data)
    sync.Once run init exactly once (lazy singleton)
    errgroup.Group like WaitGroup + first error returned; WithContext cancels the others on error 
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
var mu sync.Mutex
count := 0
for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()
        mu.Lock()
        count++
        mu.Unlock()
    }()
}
wg.Wait()
fmt.Println(count) // 100 (without the mutex: a data race, often < 100)

    // import "golang.org/x/sync/errgroup"
func fetchAll(ctx context.Context, urls []string) error {
    g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
    for _, u := range urls {
        g.Go(func() error { return fetch(ctx, u) }) // first error cancels ctx
    }
    return g.Wait() // first non-nil error
}
    ↑ top

    Gotchas: predict the output

    1. append aliasing

    a := make([]int, 3, 4) // len 3, cap 4
b := append(a, 1)      // fits in cap → shares a's array
c := append(a, 2)      // writes the same slot
fmt.Println(a, b, c)   // [0 0 0] [0 0 0 2] [0 0 0 2]

s := []int{1, 2, 3}
t := s[:2]
t = append(t, 99)      // overwrites s[2]
fmt.Println(s, t)      // [1 2 99] [1 2 99]

    Why: a slice is (pointer, len, cap). append reuses the array while len < cap; it copies only when it must grow. Fix: slices.Clone, or a full slice expression s[:2:2] (cap = len, so append must copy).

    2. Loop variable capture

    var fs []func()
for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
    fs = append(fs, func() { fmt.Print(i, " ") })
}
for _, f := range fs {
    f()
}
// Go 1.22+: 0 1 2     before 1.22: 3 3 3

    Before Go 1.22 the loop had one i shared by all closures/goroutines. Since 1.22, each iteration gets a new variable (only when go.mod says go 1.22 or later). Old fix: i := i inside the loop.

    3. Nil interface holding a nil pointer

    type MyErr struct{}

func (*MyErr) Error() string { return "boom" }

func find() error {
    var p *MyErr = nil
    return p // interface = (type=*MyErr, value=nil)
}

func main() {
    err := find()
    fmt.Println(err == nil, err) // false boom
}

    An interface is nil only if both type and value are nil. Fix: return nil explicitly.

    4. defer order and argument evaluation

    func loop() {
    for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
        defer fmt.Print(i, " ")
    }
} // prints 2 1 0 (LIFO)

func args() {
    x := 1
    defer fmt.Println("deferred:", x) // x evaluated NOW → "deferred: 1"
    x = 2
}

func named() (n int) {
    defer func() { n++ }() // can change named results
    return 1
} // returns 2

    Deferred calls run LIFO at function return; their arguments are evaluated immediately. A closure (defer func(){...}()) sees the variable's final value. defer in a loop runs only when the function returns, not each iteration (file-handle leak).

    5. Concurrent map writes

    m := map[int]int{}
for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {
    go func() { m[i] = i }() // fatal error: concurrent map writes
}

    Not a panic: a fatal error, recover can't catch it. Fix: sync.Mutex/RWMutex around the map, or sync.Map (good for mostly-read or disjoint-key workloads). Detect with go test -race.

    6. Map iteration order is randomized on purpose. Never rely on it; sort the keys (slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))).

    7. Goroutine leak on a blocked channel

    func first(urls []string) string {
    ch := make(chan string) // unbuffered
    for _, u := range urls {
        go func() { ch <- fetch(u) }()
    }
    return <-ch // the other goroutines block on send forever → leak
}

    Fix: make(chan string, len(urls)) so every send succeeds, or pass a ctx and select on ctx.Done() when sending. A leaked goroutine is never garbage-collected.

    ✓ Key points
    • "Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating": channels for hand-off, mutex for simple shared state.
    • Every goroutine you start needs a clear way to stop (close, ctx cancel).
    • Always defer cancel() after context.WithTimeout/WithCancel.
    • Run tests with -race for any concurrent code.
    ❝ Interview line

    "Goroutines are cheap user-space threads multiplexed onto OS threads by the GMP scheduler, so they run in parallel. I coordinate them with channels or sync primitives, propagate cancellation with context, and use errgroup when I need the first error and cancellation of the rest."

    ⚠ Common trap

    returning a typed nil pointer as an error (it's != nil), and starting goroutines that block forever on an unbuffered channel nobody reads. Both compile fine and only fail at runtime.

    Chapter 8 · Django

    Django Overview

    6 pages. Each card says what the page covers and its key lines; open the page for the full depth.

    Django Interview Questions

    quick-fire Django questions with short answers, grouped by topic. Each links to the deep page.

    • Count queries: lazy QuerySet, cache per object, FK in a loop = N+1, .filter() on a prefetched manager = new query.
    • update() / bulk_* skip save() and save-signals; on_commit for Celery; F() for counters.
    • select_related = JOIN (FK), prefetch_related = extra IN query (M2M / reverse FK).
    • DRF: scope in get_queryset(), object permissions don't run on list, cursor pagination for big lists.
    • Async ORM = thread wrapper; no atomic() in async code.
    Read the full page →

    Django ORM in Depth

    the ORM turns Python method chains into SQL. A QuerySet is a description of a query that runs only when you need the rows.

    • A QuerySet is lazy: it hits the DB only when evaluated (iterate, list(), len(), bool(), step-slice, repr). Its results are cached on that object.
    • select_related = SQL JOIN (FK / one-to-one, 1 query). prefetch_related = separate query + Python join (M2M / reverse FK, 1 + 1 per relation).
    • N+1 shows up in loops and serializers. Catch it with assertNumQueries / debug-toolbar.
    • F() = do the math in the DB (no lost update). Q() = OR / NOT / complex filters.
    • update(), bulk_create(), bulk_update() skip save() and pre/post_save signals.
    • get_or_create is only race-safe with a unique constraint in the DB.
    Read the full page →

    Request Lifecycle, Middleware & Signals

    how an HTTP request travels through Django, and the hooks (middleware, signals) you can plug into that path.

    • Flow: server (gunicorn/uvicorn) → WSGI/ASGI handler → middleware (top→down) → URL resolver → process_view → view → response → middleware (bottom→up).
    • Middleware is an onion: order in MIDDLEWARE matters (Session before Auth, Security first).
    • CBV: as_view() creates a new instance per request, dispatch() picks the method handler.
    • Signals are synchronous, run in the same transaction, and are not fired by update() / bulk_*.
    • Prefer explicit service functions over signals for business logic; use transaction.on_commit for side effects.
    Read the full page →

    Transactions & Migrations

    how Django manages DB transactions and row locks, and how schema changes (migrations) are created and deployed safely.

    • Default is autocommit: every query commits alone. atomic() groups them; nested atomic() = savepoint.
    • select_for_update() locks rows until the transaction ends; only works inside atomic(). skip_locked=True for job queues.
    • Start Celery tasks with transaction.on_commit(...), never directly inside a transaction.
    • Migrations: Django diffs models vs the state built from migration files, not the DB. django_migrations records what ran.
    • Zero-downtime = expand / contract: add nullable (or db_default), backfill, then constrain; rename/drop over several deploys; AddIndexConcurrently with atomic = False.
    Read the full page →

    Django REST Framework

    DRF is the standard toolkit for JSON APIs on Django: serializers (validation + conversion), views/viewsets, routers, and plug-in policies for auth, permissions, throttling, pagination, filtering and versioning.

    • Validation order: each field (to_internal_value + field validators) → validate_<field> → Meta/class validators → validate(attrs).
    • ModelSerializer does not write nested data; override create() / update().
    • SerializerMethodField that queries = N+1. Fix in get_queryset() with select_related / prefetch_related / annotate.
    • Authentication = who are you (sets request.user). Permission = are you allowed. has_object_permission runs only via get_object(), not on list.
    • Offset pagination = slow on deep pages + COUNT(*); cursor pagination = stable and fast, no page numbers.
    • Make POST safe to retry with an Idempotency-Key + unique constraint.
    Read the full page →

    Django in Production: Performance, Security, Async

    the things that decide whether a Django app survives real traffic: caching, DB connections, process model, static files, security settings, async limits, background jobs, observability and tests.

    • Cache layers: per-view (cache_page), template fragment ({% cache %}), low-level (cache.get_or_set). Hard part = invalidation (versioned keys, delete in on_commit).
    • CONN_MAX_AGE=0 (default) = new DB connection per request. Use CONN_MAX_AGE=60 + CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS, or pgbouncer / Django 5.1 "pool". Total connections = instances × workers × threads.
    • Security: DEBUG=False, ALLOWED_HOSTS, secrets from env, HTTPS settings, never f-strings in raw(), |safe only on trusted HTML. Run check --deploy.
    • Async ORM methods (aget, async for) still run the sync driver in a thread; atomic() doesn't work in async code → wrap in sync_to_async.
    • TestCase = rollback per test (fast, on_commit never fires); TransactionTestCase = real commits (slow, needed for locking / on_commit).

    Django Interview Questions

    Django interview questionsDjango quizhow many querieswhat's wrong with this codeORM questionsDRF questionsmiddleware questionstransaction questionsDjango security questionsDjango async questionsDjango deployment questions
    See also Django ORM in Depth · Request Lifecycle, Middleware & Signals · Transactions & Migrations · Django REST Framework · Django in Production: Performance, Security, Async

    What: quick-fire Django questions with short answers, grouped by topic. Each links to the deep page.

    ℹ Why it matters

    Iranian backend interviews (Digikala, Snapp, Divar, Cafe Bazaar, fintechs) usually start with fast "do you know X?" questions before going deep. Answer in 1–3 sentences, then offer detail.

    ↑ top

    ORM

    1. When does a QuerySet hit the database? Only when it's evaluated: iteration, list(), len(), bool(), step-slicing, repr(). Then the result is cached on that QuerySet object. count(), exists(), first() run their own queries. more

    2. select_related vs prefetch_related? select_related follows FK/one-to-one with a SQL JOIN (one query). prefetch_related runs a separate query per relation (WHERE id IN (...)) and joins in Python; use it for M2M and reverse FK. more

    3. How many queries?

    books = Book.objects.all()          # Book has FK author
for b in books:
    print(b.title, b.author.name)

    1 + N (one for books, one per book for its author). With .select_related("author") → 1.

    4. How many queries?

    authors = Author.objects.prefetch_related("books")
for a in authors:
    print(a.books.filter(published=True).count())

    1 + 1 + N. The prefetch runs (2 queries), but .filter() on the related manager ignores the prefetch cache and runs a new query per author. Fix: Prefetch("books", queryset=Book.objects.filter(published=True), to_attr="pub") then len(a.pub) → 2, or annotate(Count(...)) → 1.

    5. How many queries?

    qs = Order.objects.filter(status="paid")
if qs:
    total = len(qs)
    first = qs[0]
print(qs.count())

    1. if qs evaluates and caches all rows; len(), qs[0] and count() use the cache. Correct but wasteful if you only need a check: exists() loads no rows.

    6. What are F() and Q()? F("field") refers to a column inside SQL, so update(stock=F("stock") - 1) is atomic in the DB (no lost update). Q() builds OR/NOT/dynamic conditions: Q(a=1) | ~Q(b=2). more

    7. annotate vs aggregate? aggregate returns one dict for the whole queryset; annotate adds a computed value to each row (with GROUP BY). Two Counts over different joins multiply rows → use distinct=True or Subquery. more

    8. only() / defer() vs values()? only/defer still return model instances but skip columns; touching a skipped field = an extra query per object. values()/values_list() return dicts/tuples, no model overhead.

    9. Is get_or_create safe under concurrency? Only if there's a unique constraint on the lookup fields. It does SELECT → INSERT → on IntegrityError, SELECT again. Without the constraint, two requests can both insert duplicates. more

    10. How do you process 10 million rows? .iterator(chunk_size=...) (no cache, server-side cursor on Postgres), or loop over PK ranges in batches with update()/bulk_update() per batch in short transactions. Never list(Model.objects.all()). more

    ↑ top

    Models and signals

    11. Does QuerySet.update() call save() or send post_save? No. update(), bulk_create() and bulk_update() run SQL directly: no save(), no pre/post_save, no auto_now update. (qs.delete() does send pre/post_delete.) more

    12. Why can signals be dangerous? They hide side effects, run synchronously in the same transaction (before commit), slow down every save, and are skipped by bulk operations. Prefer explicit service functions for business logic. more

    13. What's wrong with this code?

    @receiver(post_save, sender=Order)
def notify(sender, instance, created, **kw):
    if created:
        send_invoice.delay(instance.id)

    If the order is created inside atomic(), the task can start before commit → DoesNotExist in the worker, or run after a rollback. Use transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_invoice.delay(instance.id)).

    ↑ top

    Request lifecycle and middleware

    14. Describe the request lifecycle. Web server (gunicorn/uvicorn) → WSGI/ASGI handler → middleware top-down → URL resolver → process_view → view → response → middleware bottom-up → request_finished (closes old DB connections). more

    15. Why does middleware order matter? Give an example. It's an onion: each layer sees what outer layers already did. AuthenticationMiddleware needs request.session, so it must come after SessionMiddleware; SecurityMiddleware goes first to redirect to HTTPS early.

    16. WSGI vs ASGI? WSGI is synchronous, one request per worker thread. ASGI is async and supports websockets and long-lived connections. Under ASGI, sync views run in a thread pool, so it only helps if your code is really async. more

    ↑ top

    Transactions

    17. What does nested atomic() do? The outer block is a transaction; each inner block is a savepoint. An exception leaving the inner block rolls back only to that savepoint. Catch it outside the inner atomic, never inside. more

    18. When do you use select_for_update? What are skip_locked and nowait? To lock rows you read and then change based on logic (balances, seats). Must be inside atomic(). skip_locked skips locked rows (job queues), nowait fails immediately instead of waiting. more

    19. What's wrong with this code?

    def withdraw(account_id, amount):
    acc = Account.objects.get(pk=account_id)
    if acc.balance >= amount:
        acc.balance -= amount
        acc.save()

    Race condition: two requests read the same balance and both withdraw (lost update, negative balance). Fix: Account.objects.filter(pk=account_id, balance__gte=amount).update(balance=F("balance") - amount) and check the returned row count, or select_for_update() inside atomic().

    20. What is ATOMIC_REQUESTS and why do many teams avoid it? It wraps every view in a transaction. Simple, but transactions last the whole request (including slow API calls), holding locks and connections longer. Explicit atomic() around the critical part is better.

    ↑ top

    Migrations

    21. How does makemigrations know what changed? It replays all existing migration files to build an in-memory model state and diffs it against your current models. It never reads the real DB. migrate checks django_migrations for what's applied. more

    22. How do you add a NOT NULL column to a big table with zero downtime? Add it nullable (or with db_default in Django 5.0+), deploy code that writes it, backfill in batches, then add NOT NULL (on Postgres via a NOT VALID check constraint + validate). Indexes with AddIndexConcurrently and atomic = False. more

    23. Why not RenameField in production? During a rolling deploy, old code still uses the old column name and crashes. Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop the old one in a later deploy.

    ↑ top

    DRF

    24. What's the serializer validation order? Each field's parsing and validators → validate_<field>() → serializer-level validators (e.g. unique together) → validate(attrs). more

    25. What's wrong with this serializer?

    class PostSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    comments_count = serializers.SerializerMethodField()
    def get_comments_count(self, obj):
        return obj.comments.count()

    One COUNT query per post (N+1). Annotate in the view: Post.objects.annotate(comments_count=Count("comments")) and use IntegerField(read_only=True).

    26. Authentication vs permission? 401 vs 403? Authentication identifies the user (sets request.user); permissions decide access. 401 = not authenticated (with a WWW-Authenticate header, e.g. token/JWT), 403 = authenticated but not allowed (or session auth). more

    27. Why isn't has_object_permission enough to protect a list endpoint? DRF calls it only from get_object() (detail routes). list() never calls it, so filter the queryset by user in get_queryset().

    28. Offset vs cursor pagination? Offset needs COUNT(*) and scans skipped rows, so deep pages are slow and inserts cause duplicates/skips. Cursor uses WHERE key < cursor on an indexed, unique ordering: fast and stable, but no total or jump-to-page. more

    29. How do you make a "create payment" POST safe to retry? Client sends an Idempotency-Key; store it with a unique constraint and the first response; on a repeat, return the stored response instead of creating again. more

    ↑ top

    Performance and deployment

    30. Your endpoint is slow. What do you check first? Query count and time (debug-toolbar / Sentry / assertNumQueries) → N+1 and missing indexes (EXPLAIN ANALYZE) → payload size and serializer cost → caching → external calls that should be async (Celery). more

    31. What do CONN_MAX_AGE and pgbouncer solve? CONN_MAX_AGE=0 opens a new DB connection per request. A positive value reuses connections per thread (add CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS). Pgbouncer (transaction mode) or Django 5.1's "pool" option limits real Postgres connections when you have many workers; with pgbouncer set DISABLE_SERVER_SIDE_CURSORS. more

    ↑ top

    Security

    32. How does Django prevent CSRF, XSS and SQL injection? CSRF: middleware checks a secret token on unsafe methods for cookie-based auth. XSS: templates auto-escape (broken by mark_safe/safe). SQL injection: ORM and params are parameterized (broken by f-strings in raw()/extra()/cursor.execute()). more

    33. Production settings checklist? DEBUG=False, real ALLOWED_HOSTS, SECRET_KEY from env, SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, secure cookies, HSTS, SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER behind a proxy, and manage.py check --deploy in CI.

    ↑ top

    Async and testing

    34. Can you use the ORM in an async view? Transactions? Yes via the async API (aget, acreate, async for), but it still runs the sync driver in a thread. atomic() doesn't work in async code: put that logic in a sync function and call it with sync_to_async. Calling the sync ORM directly raises SynchronousOnlyOperation. more

    35. TestCase vs TransactionTestCase? TestCase wraps each test in a transaction and rolls back (fast), so on_commit callbacks never run (use captureOnCommitCallbacks). TransactionTestCase really commits and truncates tables (slow); use it for locking, on_commit and multi-connection tests.

    ✓ Key points
    • Lead with the one-line answer, then the "why", then offer a code example.
    • For "how many queries" questions: find every place a lazy relation is touched in a loop.
    • For "what's wrong" questions: look for N+1, read-modify-write races, side effects before commit, and missing user scoping.
    ❝ Interview line

    "Most Django problems I've fixed in production were N+1 queries, races from read-modify-write, and Celery tasks started before commit, so I check for exactly those three in every code review."

    ⚠ Common trap

    answering only with API names ("use select_related"). Interviewers want the mechanism: what SQL runs, how many queries, and what happens under concurrency.

    Django ORM in Depth

    QuerySetlazy evaluationqueryset cacheselect_relatedprefetch_relatedPrefetchto_attrN+1assertNumQueriesdjango-debug-toolbarF expressionQ objectannotateaggregateSubqueryOuterRefExistsvaluesvalues_listonlydeferbulk_createbulk_updateupdate vs saveiteratorchunk_sizeget_or_createupdate_or_createMeta indexesUniqueConstraintraw SQLRawSQLconnection.cursor
    See also Transactions & Migrations · Django REST Framework · Django in Production: Performance, Security, Async · Indexes · Locking & Concurrency Control · Django Interview Questions · Request Lifecycle, Middleware & Signals

    What: the ORM turns Python method chains into SQL. A QuerySet is a description of a query that runs only when you need the rows.

    ℹ Why it matters

    most Django performance bugs are ORM bugs: N+1 queries, loading whole rows you don't need, read-modify-write races. Interviewers love "how many queries does this run?".

    ↑ top

    Laziness and evaluation

    qs = Book.objects.filter(published=True)   # 0 queries: nothing runs
qs = qs.exclude(price=0).order_by("-id")   # 0 queries: still building SQL
for b in qs: ...                           # 1 query: evaluated, results cached in qs
for b in qs: ...                           # 0 queries: uses qs's cache

    What evaluates a QuerySet (runs the query and fills the cache): iteration, list(qs), len(qs), bool(qs) / if qs:, slicing with a step (qs[::2]), repr(qs) (shell), pickling.

    What does NOT fill the cache (runs its own query every time):

    Call SQL Note
    qs.count() SELECT COUNT(*) uses cache if qs already evaluated
    qs.exists() SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1 cheapest "is there any?"
    qs[0], qs.first() LIMIT 1 on an unevaluated qs, a new query every call
    qs[10:20] LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10 returns a new lazy QuerySet
    qs.get(...) WHERE ... raises DoesNotExist / MultipleObjectsReturned 
    # How many queries?
qs = Book.objects.all()
if qs:                 # 1: loads ALL rows into memory just to check
    print(qs[0])       # 0: qs is already evaluated, uses cache
# Better: if qs.exists() when you don't need the rows.

print(Book.objects.all()[0])  # 1
print(Book.objects.all()[0])  # 1 again: a new QuerySet every time → 2 total

    Calling .filter() / .all() on a QuerySet returns a new QuerySet without the cache.

    ↑ top

    select_related vs prefetch_related

    select_related prefetch_related
    Relation ForeignKey, OneToOne (forward; reverse one-to-one too) ManyToMany, reverse FK (author.book_set), also FK
    SQL one query with JOIN one extra query per relation: WHERE id IN (...)
    Join done in the database Python
    Risk wide rows, big joins big IN lists, memory 
    # N+1: 1 query for books + 1 per book for author
for b in Book.objects.all():
    print(b.author.name)

# 1 query (JOIN)
for b in Book.objects.select_related("author", "author__country"):
    print(b.author.name)

# 2 queries: authors, then all their books with WHERE author_id IN (...)
for a in Author.objects.prefetch_related("books"):
    print([b.title for b in a.books.all()])

    Prefetch objects let you filter, order or select_related the inner query, and store the result in a list:

    from django.db.models import Prefetch

authors = Author.objects.prefetch_related(
    Prefetch(
        "books",
        queryset=Book.objects.filter(published=True).select_related("publisher"),
        to_attr="published_books",          # a plain list attribute
    )
)
for a in authors:                           # 2 queries total
    for b in a.published_books:
        print(b.publisher.name)

    Trap: a.books.filter(published=True) inside the loop ignores the prefetch cache and runs a new query per author. Only .all() uses the cache. Filter in the Prefetch instead.

    ↑ top

    Detecting N+1

    • django-debug-toolbar: SQL panel shows count, duplicates ("similar queries") and time per page.
    • Tests: lock the query count so a regression fails CI.
    def test_book_list_queries(self):
    with self.assertNumQueries(2):
        self.client.get("/api/books/")
# pytest-django: django_assert_num_queries(2) fixture
    • Production: Sentry performance ("N+1 query" detection), nplusone, or django-silk in staging. connection.queries works only with DEBUG=True.
    ↑ top

    F() and Q()

    F("field") refers to a column value inside SQL, so the DB does the math atomically.

    # ❌ read-modify-write: two requests both read 10 and both write 9 (lost update)
p = Product.objects.get(pk=1)
p.stock -= 1
p.save()

# ✅ one atomic UPDATE: SET stock = stock - 1
Product.objects.filter(pk=1, stock__gt=0).update(stock=F("stock") - 1)  # returns rows changed

# F also compares columns
Order.objects.filter(paid_amount__lt=F("total"))

    Q() builds OR, NOT and dynamic filters:

    from django.db.models import Q
Book.objects.filter(Q(title__icontains=s) | Q(author__name__icontains=s), ~Q(status="draft"))
    ↑ top

    annotate, aggregate, Subquery, Exists

    • aggregate() → one dict for the whole queryset ({"avg": 12.5}). It ends the chain.
    • annotate() → adds a computed column per row (GROUP BY when used with aggregates).
    from django.db.models import Count, Avg, Sum, Exists, OuterRef, Subquery

Book.objects.aggregate(avg=Avg("price"))                       # {'avg': Decimal('12.50')}
Author.objects.annotate(n=Count("books")).filter(n__gt=5)      # HAVING COUNT(...) > 5

    Trap: two Counts on different relations multiply rows (JOIN fan-out):

    # ❌ wrong numbers: books × reviews
Author.objects.annotate(b=Count("books"), r=Count("reviews"))
# ✅ distinct=True (ok for counts) or Subquery (always correct, also for Sum)
Author.objects.annotate(b=Count("books", distinct=True), r=Count("reviews", distinct=True))

    Subquery + OuterRef = a correlated subquery, e.g. "latest order date per customer":

    latest = Order.objects.filter(customer=OuterRef("pk")).order_by("-created")
Customer.objects.annotate(
    last_order_at=Subquery(latest.values("created")[:1]),
    has_open=Exists(Order.objects.filter(customer=OuterRef("pk"), status="open")),
).filter(has_open=True)

    Exists is usually faster than Count(...) > 0 or __in with a big list, because the DB can stop at the first match. In Django 3.0+ you can pass Exists(...) straight into .filter().

    ↑ top

    Loading less: values, values_list, only, defer

    Call Returns Use
    values("id", "title") dicts reports, JSON, grouping (values(...).annotate(...) = GROUP BY)
    values_list("id", flat=True) tuples / flat values lists of IDs
    only("id", "title") model instances, other fields deferred need methods but few columns
    defer("body") model instances without body skip big text/JSON columns

    Trap: accessing a deferred field later runs one extra query per object (a new N+1).

    ↑ top

    Bulk writes and update() vs save()

    Operation Queries save() called? pre/post_save signals?
    obj.save() in a loop N yes yes
    qs.update(x=...) 1 no no (also no auto_now update)
    bulk_create(objs, batch_size=1000) ~N/batch no no
    bulk_update(objs, ["x"], batch_size=1000) ~N/batch no no
    qs.delete() 1+ Model.delete() not called yes, pre/post_delete are sent (Django loads the objects to send them and handle cascades)
    • bulk_create sets PKs on the objects on PostgreSQL (uses RETURNING). Options: ignore_conflicts=True, or update_conflicts=True, unique_fields=[...], update_fields=[...] for upsert.
    • bulk_update builds a big CASE WHEN statement; it is slower than people think on large sets. For one value on many rows, update() is best.
    • If a field has auto_now=True, update() won't touch it; set it yourself: update(status="x", updated_at=timezone.now()).
    ↑ top

    Big tables: iterator()

    for row in Event.objects.filter(day=today).iterator(chunk_size=2000):
    process(row)
    • Streams rows without filling the queryset cache, so memory stays flat. On PostgreSQL it uses a server-side cursor.
    • With prefetch_related, you must pass chunk_size (prefetch runs per chunk).
    • Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, server-side cursors break → set DISABLE_SERVER_SIDE_CURSORS: True in the DB settings.
    • For updates over millions of rows, process by PK ranges (filter(pk__gt=last_id).order_by("pk")[:1000]) in small transactions.
    ↑ top

    get_or_create / update_or_create races

    obj, created = Tag.objects.get_or_create(name="python", defaults={"color": "blue"})

    How it works: SELECT → if missing, INSERT inside a savepoint → on IntegrityError it SELECTs again. So:

    • With a unique constraint on name: two parallel calls are safe; one inserts, the other gets the IntegrityError, catches it, and reads the row.
    • Without a unique constraint: both SELECTs miss, both INSERT → duplicates, and later get() raises MultipleObjectsReturned.

    update_or_create locks the row with select_for_update() inside a transaction, then updates or creates (same unique-constraint rule for the create path). Django 5.0 added create_defaults= for values used only on create.

    ↑ top

    Indexes and constraints in Meta

    class Order(models.Model):
    customer = models.ForeignKey(Customer, on_delete=models.CASCADE)  # FK gets an index automatically
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20)
    created = models.DateTimeField(db_index=True)

    class Meta:
        indexes = [
            models.Index(fields=["customer", "-created"], name="order_cust_created_idx"),
            models.Index(fields=["created"], name="order_open_idx",
                         condition=Q(status="open")),           # partial index (Postgres)
        ]
        constraints = [
            models.UniqueConstraint(fields=["customer", "external_id"], name="uniq_ext_id"),
            models.CheckConstraint(condition=Q(total__gte=0), name="total_non_negative"),
        ]

    Composite index column order matters (leftmost prefix). See indexes. Note: CheckConstraint(condition=...) is the Django 5.1+ name; older versions use check=.

    ↑ top

    Raw SQL when the ORM is not enough

    Use it for window functions you can't express, CTEs, DISTINCT ON edge cases, or tuned reporting queries.

    # Model instances from raw SQL: always pass params, never f-strings
Book.objects.raw("SELECT * FROM shop_book WHERE price > %s", [min_price])

from django.db import connection
with connection.cursor() as cur:
    cur.execute("SELECT status, count(*) FROM shop_order WHERE created > %s GROUP BY 1", [since])
    rows = cur.fetchall()

    Also available: RawSQL("...", params) inside annotate, and Func / Window expressions (Django has Window, RowNumber, Rank, Lag). Check generated SQL with print(qs.query) or qs.explain(analyze=True).

    ✓ Key points
    • QuerySets are lazy and cached per object; exists()/count() for checks, not if qs.
    • FK → select_related; M2M / reverse FK → prefetch_related (+ Prefetch to filter). Filtering a prefetched manager breaks the cache.
    • Use F() for counters and balances; it's an atomic UPDATE, not read-modify-write.
    • Bulk operations and update() skip save() and save-signals; qs.delete() still sends delete signals.
    • Multiple Counts across joins give wrong numbers; use distinct=True or Subquery.
    • Race safety comes from DB constraints, not from Python checks.
    ❝ Interview line

    "QuerySets are lazy; they hit the DB only on evaluation and cache the result. To avoid N+1 I use select_related for foreign keys, which is a JOIN, and prefetch_related for many-to-many or reverse relations, which is one extra IN query, and I lock the query count with assertNumQueries. For counters I use F() so the update is atomic in the database."

    ⚠ Common trap

    obj.counter = F("counter") + 1; obj.save() is atomic, but obj.counter now holds an expression, not a number. Saving the object again applies +1 again. Call obj.refresh_from_db() after it.
